The assistant, holding privileged access to tenant data, was induced to pull sensitive content and emit it inside an auto-fetched markdown image reference, exfiltrating the data through the rendering path. cases.title: SpAIware - Prompt Injection That Persists in Assistant Memory
cases.affects: ChatGPT memory (macOS app) - no catalogued endpoint tool
cases.basis: Publicly reproducible research by Johann Rehberger with a documented vendor fix, subsequently adopted into the MITRE ATLAS technique set as AI Agent Context Poisoning - Memory (AML.T0080.000).
cases.summary: An injected instruction, delivered through a malicious site or a booby-trapped document, is committed to ChatGPT's persistent memory and directs the assistant to end all future responses with a markdown image whose URL carries the previous question and answer as parameters. Because it lives in memory rather than in a conversation, it survives session resets and applies to every subsequent chat until memory is purged. iocs.description: The same primitive in coding agents - an on-disk file that is context every run

response_actions: Acquire the memory store before touching the host. Memory is the persistence mechanism, and it is the step responders skip.

A team can clean the host, rotate every credential and remove the malicious integration, and the agent will re-execute the attacker's instruction on its next invocation because nobody looked at the memory store. cases.title: AI Recommendation Poisoning - Memory Manipulation for Profit
cases.affects: Assistant memory stores - no catalogued endpoint tool
cases.basis: One reporting party for what was measured. Microsoft's Defender Security Research team published the counts and the observation window; the trade press repeats them and the ATLAS case study cites the Microsoft post alone, so neither is a second observation. This entry was rated high until November 2026 on the strength of that coverage and should not have been. What is independently documented is narrower: the technique and ready-made tooling for it were published by the tools' own authors from mid-2025, seven months before Microsoft's report, including a package that tells site owners to ask the assistant to remember their brand. That shows the mechanism is real and deployed. It does not show that any assistant stored a memory, and Microsoft notes that some behaviours it had seen could no longer be reproduced.
cases.contested: The source disagrees with itself on the count. Its introduction gives over 50 unique prompts from 31 companies across 14 industries, and its scope section gives 50 distinct examples from 31 companies across more than a dozen industries. Treat the figures as approximate.
cases.summary: Microsoft documented memory poisoning used for commercial gain rather than espionage. Because major assistants support pre-populating a prompt through URL parameters, an "Ask AI" or "Summarize with AI" button - or a link in a page or email - can carry an instruction the assistant parses and commits to memory, biasing later recommendations toward the party that planted it. Microsoft identified 31 companies across 14 industries deploying the technique, and observed more than 50 distinct prompts in a single data source over 60 days. Instructions embedded in documents, emails and web pages produce the same effect when the content is processed by an assistant.

response_actions: Reason about provenance rather than content: for each memory entry, establish which turn wrote it and whether the source was the user or a retrieved document.
Pull browser history and referrer logs for parameterised assistant URLs in the window; that is where the write originates.
Review memory entries that name a specific vendor, product or source as trusted, and treat those as candidates regardless of how benign they read.

Widen the threat model in reporting: the same persistence primitive supports fraud, which changes who is targeted and how often.
cases.lesson: The poisoned entry looks exactly like a legitimate stored preference, which defeats keyword triage and forces the investigator into provenance reasoning - which turn wrote this, and was the source a user or a retrieved document. It also demonstrates that memory poisoning is not only an espionage primitive; a commercial motive means far more victims and far more routine occurrence than a targeted-attack framing would predict.

Zou et al. formulate knowledge corruption as an optimisation problem, with black-box and white-box variants, and show that injecting five adversarial texts per target question into a knowledge base of millions reliably causes the system to return an attacker-chosen answer, at around a 90% success rate. cases.title: s1ngularity - A Supply-Chain Payload That Used the Victim's Own AI CLIs
cases.date_range: 2025-08-21 (workflow compromised) to 2025-08-26 (malicious versions live about four hours)
cases.basis: The Nx maintainers' own GitHub security advisory documents the affected versions, the timeline, /tmp/inventory.txt, the s1ngularity-repository exfiltration naming and the shell-profile change. The specific AI CLIs and the flags used to invoke them are not stated in the advisory text retrieved for this entry. They come from independent analyses by Wiz, Snyk and StepSecurity, which agree with one another, so that part of the record is third-party corroborated rather than vendor-documented.
cases.summary: A command-injection flaw in the Nx repository's pull-request workflow let an attacker obtain the npm publish token and push trojanised versions of the nx build system and several @nx plugins. Their postinstall script checked which AI coding CLIs were installed. It then ran Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Amazon Q with the flag that disables tool approval, and prompted them to search the filesystem for configuration, key and wallet files. The results went to /tmp/inventory.txt and were published, base64-encoded, to a public repository under the victim's own GitHub account. It also appended a shutdown command to the victim's shell profiles. The Nx Console VS Code extension installed the latest nx during version checks, so some victims were infected without ever running an npm install.

iocs.description: Affected versions per the Nx advisory
Secret inventory written by the AI CLI run; its presence proves the payload executed
Exfiltration destination created under the victim's own account - check the GitHub audit log
Shell profile modification

iocs.value: claude --dangerously-skip-permissions, gemini --yolo, q --trust-all-tools started by node from an npm lifecycle script
iocs.description: The AI CLIs did the reconnaissance; the parent process is the evidence

response_actions.action: Search every developer host and CI runner for /tmp/inventory.txt and for AI CLI processes whose parent was node, npm or the Nx Console extension host during the window.
Search the organisation's GitHub audit log and every member account for repositories named s1ngularity-repository.
Remove the added lines from .bashrc and .zshrc, uninstall the affected nx versions and clear the npm, yarn and pnpm caches.

Rotate everything the inventory could have reached: GitHub tokens and the GitHub CLI OAuth grant, npm tokens, SSH keys, cloud keys and every AI provider API key found by the catalog's credential rows.
Treat an installed AI CLI as a capability any local process can borrow. Remove bypass flags from shell aliases and wrappers, and alert when a package manager starts one.

cases.lesson: The malware shipped no scanner. It borrowed the developer's agent, which already had filesystem access, and passed it the one flag that removes the human from the loop. That makes the agent's own session store part of the crime scene. The prompt and every file the agent opened may sit in its transcript, which is why the catalog's session-log rows for these three tools belong in the collection order here.

cases.title: Tampered Claude Code Extension in Cursor's Marketplace - An SSH Backdoor Through an AI Tool's Update Channel
cases.date_range: 29 Oct 2026, about 02:27 to 13:35 PDT, as Cursor reported it
cases.affects: AIRT-0002
cases.basis: Three parties from their own evidence, each read from the page. Cursor, whose marketplace served the builds, published a security notice with the package hashes and a later update giving the cause. Microsoft Security Research analysed the extension and published the host indicators. A supply-chain security vendor compared the tampered bundle byte for byte against the clean build it had downloaded itself. The three agree on the versions, the window, the destination address and the artifacts. What rests on Cursor alone is the cause and the ceiling on affected users, and no party reports an operator using the access. The model was not involved at any stage: this is conventional malware delivered through an AI tool's extension channel, recorded because the extension directory of a catalogued tool is where the evidence sits.
cases.contested: Where the tampering happened was misreported at first. Early accounts pointed at Open VSX, the registry Cursor's marketplace mirrors, and were withdrawn. Cursor's update of 13 November says an attacker used a credential stolen from data exposed in an internal system to place the tampered copies directly on the cache that serves its marketplace, and that the upstream registry never held them. That is Cursor's account of its own systems and nobody outside can check it. The same update puts the ceiling at 5,000 users, a count of who could have received a build and not of hosts where the backdoor worked. Only two platform builds were tampered, Apple-silicon macOS and 64-bit Windows, so a Linux or Intel Mac host on the affected version numbers is not evidence of compromise.
cases.summary: On 29 October 2026, from about 02:27 to 13:35 PDT by Cursor's account, Cursor's extension marketplace served tampered builds 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 of the extension published as anthropic.claude-code. Microsoft reports that on load the extension profiled the host and reported to a remote address, added an SSH key to the user's authorized keys, tried to enable the SSH service, opened a reverse tunnel to the same address and wrote persistence for the tunnel: a LaunchAgent on macOS, a crontab entry on Linux, a scheduled task or Startup-folder script on Windows. The Visual Studio Marketplace listing and the npm package @anthropic-ai/claude-code were not affected, and Anthropic told Microsoft its systems were not compromised and that it did not build the package. Cursor reported that errors and the need for administrator rights stopped SSH access on most macOS and Windows hosts. Cursor later gave the cause as a stolen credential used to write to the cache that serves its marketplace, with at most 5,000 users exposed and the last attacker activity on 1 November. An independent comparison found the tampered file to be the clean 2.1.312 bundle with one unobfuscated loader of about 7 KB placed in front of it, and the build labelled 2.1.313 still identifying itself internally as 2.1.312, so the version a host reports is not a reliable test. Nobody attributes the activity.

response_actions.action: List installed Cursor extensions with their versions on every host that ran Cursor on 29 October 2026, and find anthropic.claude-code at 2.1.312 or 2.1.313, recording where each copy was installed from. Then hash extension.js in each copy and compare it with the published value, because the version alone clears nothing and condemns nothing. On those hosts, before removing anything, collect the extension folder, the authorized_keys files, the persistence artifacts and the .stk_ file, then block the remote address and stop any ssh or autossh process carrying the reverse-forward arguments.

Remove the added key by fingerprint, the LaunchAgent, crontab entry, scheduled task and Startup script, the .smt and .smtk files, and the tampered extension. Check whether the SSH service was enabled by the extension and was not on before.

Treat every credential reachable from that user's session as exposed on any host where the tunnel connected, and rotate them. Where the SSH step failed, the profiling beacon still ran, so the host's details were disclosed.

Pin or allow-list editor extensions and their marketplaces on managed hosts, and alert on a code editor's process tree adding an SSH key or creating autostart entries. Cursor documents an extension allowlist and an install delay for new versions; a delay of a day would have outlasted this window.

cases.lesson: An AI coding tool's extension folder is a software supply chain of its own, with a marketplace that is not the one the vendor of the extension publishes to. The same extension id was clean in one marketplace and tampered in another, so the id proves nothing and the version and install source decide it, and here not even the version did, since one build misreported its own. The catalog has no row for Cursor's extension directory yet, because the vendor documents no path for it and none has been confirmed on a host. The rule this case links to matches the reverse tunnel it opened; it was written for this case and has not been fired against real events.

cases.title: Storm-0940 and ARTEX - A Vendor's Application Identities Used Against Its Customers' Tenants
cases.date_range: Sep 2026 (first ARTEX use Microsoft reports) to 18 Oct 2026; password spray 10 to 14 Oct, application sign-ins 15 Oct, vendor identities disabled 17 Oct 07:00 UTC
cases.affects: Microsoft Entra ID tenants reached through a vendor's multitenant applications - no catalogued endpoint tool
cases.basis: Two layers with different support. That a vendor's application identities were used to sign in to its customers' tenants is established by four parties writing from their own data: the vendor's advisory, two managed security providers who watched it in their customers' sign-in logs, and Microsoft. A cloud security vendor separately reports the same addresses and tooling against other software vendors. That an AI agent drove it, and that the operator was Storm-0940, rests on Microsoft alone: the vendor says its attribution relies on intelligence Microsoft shared, and both providers say their telemetry is consistent with Microsoft's account and does not confirm it. The entry stays medium for that reason, because the AI is why the case is in this catalog. No source names a model or says where the framework ran. The AI ran on the actor's side, so a victim tenant holds sign-in and audit records and nothing that shows a model was involved.
cases.contested: How much of this an agent did. Microsoft describes little human interaction. One responder puts an LLM's involvement at low-to-medium confidence on its own telemetry, medium-to-high given Microsoft's attribution, and reads the activity as scripted tooling steered by an operator. Its strongest evidence against full autonomy is that after one service principal was deleted, requests using it kept arriving every few seconds for 22 minutes, were rejected every time and never changed. It also notes that Microsoft does not say how it identified ARTEX or what ties the earlier password spray to the actor. The numbers measure different things and should not be added: Microsoft counts more than 2,250 tenants attempted; one provider counts almost 1,000 tenants with sign-in activity and over 300 successful among its own customers; the vendor gives no count. On outcome, Microsoft says a successful sign-in does not show data was taken, one provider saw tokens issued and nothing visibly taken, and another advises treating the application's data as exposed. The sources also disagree on which addresses did what: Microsoft lists three for application sign-ins, while one responder saw application sign-ins from 144.172.64[.]128 only and user password spraying from the others. Microsoft lists three application ids, the vendor disabled seven and names an eighth, and the root cause at the vendor was still under investigation when its advisory was last updated.

actors.stated_confidence: "Microsoft assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible"; no confidence level is given

victims.basis: Microsoft lists the industries the actor targets and counts "hundreds of organizations globally" for the ARTEX-driven activity, more than 2,250 tenants for sign-in attempts through the vendor's applications, and 327 accounts in eight organisations for the password spray. One managed security provider counts almost 1,000 tenants with sign-in activity and over 300 with a successful sign-in among its own customers. Nobody names a country or gives a count of organisations compromised.

cases.summary: Microsoft reports that Storm-0940, which it describes as a China-state aligned actor, has used ARTEX since at least September 2026 to automate attacks on hundreds of organisations. ARTEX is described as an open-source, multi-agent penetration-testing framework that can drive any model and runs a test from reconnaissance to exfiltration with little human input. In October the actor obtained credentials for several ConnectWise cloud applications, among them Cloud Backup, and used the consent customers had already granted those applications to sign in to their tenants. The vendor dates its discovery to 14 October and disabled the affected identities on 17 October at 07:00 UTC. Responders watching customer tenants saw the application sign-ins on 15 October between about 06:13 and 08:34 UTC, from one address, presenting a client assertion, and arriving in ascending order of tenant id one to six minutes apart, which is what a script walking a sorted list looks like. Where a sign-in succeeded, the reported follow-on was reconnaissance through Microsoft Graph, credentials added to applications for persistence, an application assigning itself Global Administrator, bulk reads of Key Vault secrets and mail access. One responder saw the persistence steps come from private Azure addresses, not from the published ones. A password spray on 10 to 14 October hit 327 accounts in eight organisations and, by Microsoft's account, authenticated to none. Microsoft says some intrusions went from first targeting to privileged access in under three hours.

response_actions.action: Keep the affected vendor connections disabled, and do not delete the enterprise applications as the first step - the vendor's own guidance says the same, because deletion removes the configuration and the service principal the evidence is keyed to. Export Entra sign-in and audit logs, Microsoft 365 audit records and Graph activity logs now, because the default retention is days to weeks. Inventory all eight application ids in every tenant where they were ever consented to, including tenants that no longer use the product.

Review service principal sign-ins for those applications from at least 1 October, successful and failed separately, and do not limit the review to the published addresses - the persistence activity one responder saw came from private Azure addresses. In the audit log, look for credentials, owners, role assignments and consent grants added by or to those applications, and to any other application in the tenant on the same days, and remove the ones nobody can account for once they are recorded.

Rotate every secret in any Key Vault the applications could read and treat mail and files the applications could reach as exposed where post-sign-in activity is found. Confirm with the vendor that the replacement identities no longer use a shared secret before re-enabling the connection - it reports moving to federated credentials - and check that backup and restore still work.

Review what each multitenant vendor application is permitted to do in the tenant and reduce it, alert on credential additions and role assignments made by applications, and restrict application sign-ins by location where the licence allows.

cases.lesson: The AI in this case ran on the actor's infrastructure, so there is no agent transcript, config file or token on a victim host to collect, and the catalog has no row for it. What the victim holds is identity-provider logging with a short retention clock, which is why the telemetry tab lists it as a source of its own. It is also the case to read before repeating a headline about autonomous attacks: the parties who watched it in tenant logs could confirm the intrusion and could not confirm the agent, and the one detail that speaks to autonomy cuts against it. Evidence in the tenant answers what was done and when. Whether a model chose to do it is on the actor's server.

cases.title: ARTEX Harvests Exposed Secrets From Public Repositories and Signs In as the Application
cases.date_range: Aug 2026 (repository searches first observed) onward; application sign-ins from 28 Oct 2026, still under way on 3 Nov 2026
cases.affects: Application secrets and AI service keys exposed in public repositories, and the Entra ID and Azure resources they unlock - no catalogued endpoint tool
cases.basis: Two parties writing from their own data, both read from the page. A managed security provider published the campaign on 3 November from what it saw in its customers' tenants, and Microsoft's post two days later credits that report and adds the repository searches and the framework. The intrusion, its scale and the data taken are the provider's first-hand account. That an agentic framework drove it is Microsoft's: the provider first put AI involvement at low confidence and then said Microsoft's findings matched its assessment, which is agreement and not a second observation. Nobody attributes the activity to an actor. Microsoft calls the network indicators unattributed and two of the addresses only "potentially associated", and no source names a model or says where the framework ran.
cases.contested: Whether this is the same operation as the October compromise of a backup vendor's applications (AIRT-CS-0024). The provider that saw both assesses them as unrelated. Microsoft places both under the same framework and attributes this one to nobody, and a shared open-source tool is not a shared operator. The two sources also describe one address differently: Microsoft flags 199.19.77[.]18 as a Tor exit node, and the provider reports password spraying through the Azure command-line client from it and from 65.87.223[.]26, linked to the operator with low to moderate confidence.

victims.basis: One provider's count among its own customers: about 45 application registrations in about 18 organisations targeted, more than 33 authenticated, and 27 organisations reached once downstream tenants are included. It lists government, energy, food and agriculture, transportation, construction and engineering, legal, education and nonprofits; construction has no term in this vocabulary and is left out. Microsoft gives no count, sector or country. Neither figure is the size of the campaign.

cases.summary: Microsoft reports that from August 2026 an agentic offensive framework, ARTEX, sent large volumes of searches to GitHub for secrets, combining a target organisation's name with secret, cloud-service and AI-provider keywords. It looked for application credentials and for API keys to AI services, which the post says the agents sought out repeatedly. From 28 October the harvested application credentials were used for service principal sign-ins to Entra ID across dozens of applications in several tenants, followed by discovery of subscriptions, permissions and AI model deployments, reads of storage keys, connection strings and Key Vault secrets, searches of Azure DevOps, SharePoint and mailbox access, and scripts run on virtual machines through Run Command. In one tenant a vendor-owned multitenant application's credential, compromised at the vendor, gave access to downstream tenants. Microsoft describes one run that went from searching GitHub for a client secret to exfiltrating from a Key Vault in five minutes, and requests that failed and were reissued against a different API version within about half a minute. A managed security provider that watched the same addresses in its customers' tenants reports what was taken: searches of SharePoint and mail in about 25 tenants, 81 files downloaded and roughly 2,279 mailbox items read, with one address making 412 sign-in attempts in seven days from 1 November. One of its partners was billed thousands of dollars of AI service usage in about ten minutes.

Block the published address for workload identities where the licence allows, knowing the policy covers only single-tenant applications in the tenant and that already-issued tokens stay valid until they expire.

For every application that signed in from those addresses or logged the two secret errors, remove all client secrets, certificates and federated credentials, including any the actor added, and disable the service principal if it cannot be re-credentialed at once. Revoke sessions, Azure DevOps personal access tokens and SSH keys for affected users.

Rotate everything in any Key Vault the application could read, every storage key and connection string it could list, and any AI service key it could reach, then review Run Command history on virtual machines the application had rights over. Check the bill for AI services on the days in question - one affected organisation was charged thousands of dollars in about ten minutes - and treat mail and files the application could search as read. Managed service providers should also review partner access and customer tenants.

Treat any secret that was ever in a public repository as compromised - removing the commit does not invalidate it. Turn on secret scanning and push protection, set maximum lifetimes for application passwords, and move applications from client secrets to managed identities or federated credentials.

cases.lesson: The catalog lists where AI tools keep API keys on a host because those files are what gets copied into a repository. This case is the other end of that: an agent that searches public code for exactly those keys and for application secrets, and uses one within minutes. No catalogued tool ran on the victim's side, so the evidence is the provider's sign-in and resource logs, and the AI is visible only in the speed and in the way failed requests were corrected.

No second party has reported on Storm-3358 from its own data: an FBI FLASH of 13 November reprints these indicators and credits them to Microsoft, which is distribution and not corroboration. Other parties do report on the framework, from operator consoles and from intrusions by other users of it, and the framework artefacts listed below come from those reports and were not observed for this actor. The post gives no victim count, no outcome, no vulnerability identifier and no host artifact for any of the three remote-access tools it names. It names no model and says only that some published addresses are ARTEX servers. Its figure showing the download commands is an image whose text could not be read for this entry. On any server that contacted them, capture memory and the process tree before restarting anything, since none of the three tools has a published on-disk indicator.

On affected web servers, list files created by the web server's account in the upload and temporary directories, cron entries and services added since the first contact, and outbound connections that persist. Remove what is found and close the upload or request-forgery flaw that let it in.

Rotate credentials stored on or reachable from the compromised servers, including database and cloud credentials in application configuration, and review authentication from those servers to internal systems for the lateral movement the post reports.
Require authentication on file upload endpoints, restrict what internet-facing applications may request on the server's behalf, and alert when a web server process starts a download tool or a shell.

cases.lesson: This is the case the guide's "where did the AI run" section exists for. The agent was on the actor's server and what reached the victim was scanning, an exploited web application and a conventional remote-access tool, so the catalog has no row and the investigation is an ordinary web server compromise run faster. The published indicators are all network addresses with a short life, and one of them is printed two ways in the source. The one rule linked here matches a default file name the framework leaves, taken from another party's intrusion report, which makes it a tripwire for a careless operator and nothing more.
